founder_b: John Sculley (CEO hired 1983, not a cofounder)
what_happened: After Jobs lost a May 1985 power struggle with CEO John Sculley, Apple's board sided with Sculley and moved Jobs out of the Macintosh group, and Jobs resigned on 17 September 1985.
notes: In substance a board ouster of a founder, but excluded from cofounder-pair counts because Sculley was hired, not a cofounder. Sculley (2015): the board 'deemed Jobs' presence in the company too disruptive'.

what_happened: Ronald Wayne withdrew from the Apple partnership about 12 days after signing it in April 1976 and sold his 10% stake back to Jobs and Wozniak for $800, fearing personal liability for the partnership's debts.
notes: Wozniak has said Wayne left after a few months, not 12 days; Wayne took a further $1,500 in 1977 to waive future claims. No conflict documented.

what_happened: Wozniak left day-to-day work at Apple in early 1985, saying the company had been going in the wrong direction for five years, but he left amicably and says he never came off Apple's employee list.
notes: Wikipedia (Steve Jobs article): 'Wozniak left amicably and remained an honorary employee of Apple.' No documented conflict with Jobs over the departure.

what_happened: Allen resigned from Microsoft on 18 February 1983 after, by his own account, overhearing Gates and Steve Ballmer in December 1982 discussing how to dilute his equity; Gates then offered to buy his shares for $5 each and Allen refused.
notes: Borderline: Allen's Hodgkin's diagnosis in 1982 was the trigger and the acrimony became public only in his 2011 memoir Idea Man (Vanity Fair excerpt); the two reconciled and stayed friends until Allen's death in 2018.

what_happened: In 2005 Zuckerberg restructured Facebook so that Saverin's stake was diluted and pushed him out of the company; Facebook sued Saverin over the 2005 stock agreement, Saverin countersued, and the parties settled in 2009 with Saverin keeping his cofounder credit.
notes: Settlement terms confidential; Business Insider (May 2012) published Zuckerberg's emails on diluting Saverin toward 10%.

what_happened: Hughes, who had left Facebook in 2007 to join the Obama campaign, published a New York Times op-ed on 9 May 2019 calling for the government to break up Facebook and curb Zuckerberg's power, and said a month later that he had not heard from Zuckerberg since.
notes: Borderline: a public policy dispute with no lawsuit or ouster; Hughes said he had 'no personal, negative feelings for Mark'. His 2007 departure itself was quiet.

what_happened: Moskovitz, Facebook's first chief technology officer, announced on 3 October 2008 that he was leaving to found Asana with Justin Rosenstein; no conflict with Zuckerberg is documented.
notes: Wikipedia only; no news source fetched (search budget exhausted). Andrew McCollum (left 2007) not researched.

what_happened: Evan Williams fired Noah Glass, the Odeo founder who named Twitter and championed it, in late 2006 after buying Odeo back from its investors, and Glass's role as a Twitter cofounder went unacknowledged until 2011.
notes: Glass and early employees told Business Insider he was pushed out partly because he wanted to run Twitter himself; Nick Bilton's Hatching Twitter (2013) reports Dorsey asked Williams to remove him, not verifiable here (NYT blocked).

what_happened: In October 2008 Evan Williams and Twitter's board pushed Jack Dorsey out as CEO, Williams took the job himself and Dorsey became a non-employee chairman; the two have rarely spoken since beyond board meetings.
notes: Williams became CEO on 16 October 2008. Dorsey (Vanity Fair, 2011): 'It was like being punched in the stomach.'

what_happened: Williams handed the CEO job to Dick Costolo on 4 October 2010, publicly as his own decision to focus on product; Nick Bilton's 2013 book reports the board pushed him out with Dorsey lobbying against him, which could not be confirmed from a fetchable source.
notes: TechCrunch and Wikipedia record only the voluntary framing; the New York Times excerpt of Hatching Twitter (13 Oct 2013) is blocked to this tool. Dorsey returned as executive chairman in March 2011.

what_happened: In August 2007 Tesla's board, led by chairman Elon Musk, asked cofounder and CEO Martin Eberhard to step down; Eberhard sued Musk for libel and breach of contract in June 2009, dropped the suit in August, and a September 2009 settlement lets five people, including Musk, call themselves Tesla cofounders.
notes: Eberhard left the company in January 2008. Wired (19 Aug 2009) on the withdrawal; Business Insider (Feb 2023) confirms the settlement. Marc Tarpenning, Ian Wright and JB Straubel left without documented conflict (not researched).

what_happened: Five major investors led by Benchmark demanded Kalanick's resignation in a letter and he stepped down as Uber CEO on 20 June 2017; cofounder Garrett Camp took no public position against him.
notes: Investor-driven after the Holder report on harassment; Kalanick stayed on the board until 2019.

what_happened: After its IPO filing drew scorn, WeWork's board, with largest investor SoftBank, pressed Neumann to step aside and he resigned as CEO on 24 September 2019, later leaving the board with a SoftBank exit package; cofounder Miguel McKelvey took no public position against him.
notes: Exit package reported at about $1.7bn in October 2019, renegotiated in 2021. CNBC (24 Sep 2019) on the co-CEO successors also fetched.

what_happened: While Musk was away on his honeymoon in September 2000, X.com's executives moved against his leadership and the board replaced him as CEO with Peter Thiel in October 2000.
notes: Musk founded X.com; Thiel and Levchin founded Confinity; the two merged in March 2000 and all are counted as PayPal cofounders. CNBC relays Musk's own account of the honeymoon coup.

what_happened: Brown, who says he had the original idea for Snapchat, was cut out by Spiegel and Murphy in 2011, sued them in February 2013, and settled in September 2014 for $157.5 million with Snapchat crediting him with the concept.
notes: Spiegel and Murphy described Brown as an unpaid intern; the $157.5m figure is in Snap's February 2017 S-1 (Note on legal proceedings).

what_happened: Wolfe Herd left Tinder in April 2014 and in June 2014 sued Tinder, IAC, Justin Mateen and Sean Rad for sexual harassment and discrimination, saying she had been stripped of her cofounder title; Mateen was suspended and the case settled in September 2014 for just over $1 million.
notes: Cofounder status disputed: Rad and TechCrunch's 2014 reporting say she was not a cofounder; she maintains she 'is, was, and will always be' one. Business Insider (4 Nov 2014) on the settlement amount.

what_happened: Conrad resigned as Zenefits CEO on 8 February 2016 after an internal investigation found the company's insurance licensing out of compliance; COO David Sacks, also an investor, took over as CEO and cofounder Laks Srini stayed.
notes: No fetched source names a board vote; Sacks' email to staff: 'As a result, Parker has resigned.' Classed as board ouster per the brief.

what_happened: Swartz, who became a Reddit co-owner when his Infogami merged into it in late 2005, was fired by acquirer Conde Nast/Wired in January 2007 after he stopped coming into the office following the sale.
notes: Fired by the acquirer, not by his cofounders; Ohanian publicly disputed Swartz's cofounder title in 2011. Cofounder status disputed.

what_happened: Systrom and Krieger resigned from Instagram together on 24 September 2018 amid reported tensions with Mark Zuckerberg over Instagram's autonomy; there was no split between the two cofounders.
notes: Founders-versus-acquirer event, not a cofounder breakup.

what_happened: Acton left WhatsApp in September 2017 after a dispute with Facebook over monetization, forfeiting about $850 million in unvested stock, and Koum left in April 2018 over privacy disagreements with Facebook; the two cofounders did not split from each other.
notes: Founders-versus-acquirer event. CNBC (13 Sep 2017) and the Guardian (30 Apr 2018) also fetched.

founder_b: Facebook (acquirer); cofounders Brendan Iribe; Michael Antonov; Nate Mitchell stayed
what_happened: Luckey left Facebook-owned Oculus in March 2017 after the controversy over his 2016 donation to a pro-Trump group; the Wall Street Journal later reported he was put on leave and fired with a payout of at least $100 million, and Zuckerberg told the Senate in 2018 it 'was not because of a political view'.
notes: Pushed out by the owner, Facebook, not by cofounders. Ars Technica (30 Mar 2017) and The Verge (10 Apr 2018) also fetched.

founder_b: Board (CEO John Morgridge; Sequoia's Don Valentine)
what_happened: Lerner was fired from Cisco on 28 August 1990 by the management that investor Don Valentine of Sequoia had installed, and her husband and cofounder Len Bosack resigned the same day in protest.
notes: The two cofounders left together; they later divorced.

what_happened: On 17 November 2023 OpenAI's board, with cofounder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever reportedly leading the push, fired CEO Sam Altman; cofounder Greg Brockman quit in protest, Sutskever posted that he 'deeply regretted' his participation, and Altman was reinstated on 21-22 November.
notes: Sutskever left OpenAI in May 2024. Ars Technica (18 Nov 2023) and The Verge (17 Nov 2023, Brockman) also fetched.

what_happened: Musk left OpenAI's board in February 2018 citing a conflict with Tesla's AI work, sued Altman and OpenAI in 2024 claiming they broke the promise to stay a nonprofit, had a $97.4bn bid for the nonprofit rejected in February 2025, and lost at trial in May 2026 when a jury found his claims time-barred.
notes: The Verge (21 Feb 2018) and the Guardian (14 Feb 2025) also fetched; Musk called the verdict a 'calendar technicality' and said he would appeal.

what_happened: Balwani joined Theranos in 2009 as president and COO, six years after Holmes founded it alone; the two were tried separately and both were convicted of fraud in 2022.
notes: Holmes convicted January 2022, Balwani July 2022; sentenced to nearly 13 years in December 2022.

what_happened: FTX cofounder Gary Wang pleaded guilty to fraud in December 2022, cooperated with prosecutors and testified against Bankman-Fried at his October 2023 trial, which ended in a conviction on all counts on 2 November 2023.
notes: Guardian (21 Dec 2022) on the plea also fetched; Wang received no prison time in November 2024.

what_happened: After rejecting Microsoft's $47.5bn bid, Yang announced on 17 November 2008 that he would step down as Yahoo CEO as the board faced intensifying pressure from shareholders led by Carl Icahn; cofounder David Filo stayed and took no public position.
notes: Framed by Yahoo as Yang's own decision; Yang stayed on the board until January 2012. TIME (19 Nov 2008) also fetched.

what_happened: Groupon's board fired CEO Andrew Mason on 28 February 2013 after missed earnings; cofounder and executive chairman Eric Lefkofsky and vice chairman Ted Leonsis took over as co-CEOs, and Lefkofsky became permanent CEO in August 2013.
notes: Borderline with board ouster: classed as a cofounder split because cofounder Lefkofsky led the board that removed Mason and took his job. Mason's memo: 'I was fired today.' NBC News (2 Jul 2013) also fetched.

what_happened: Michael Dell founded the company alone in 1984 as PC's Limited; Wikipedia names no cofounder.
notes: Solo founder, no pair; Wikipedia only.

what_happened: Jeff Bezos founded Amazon alone on 5 July 1994; Wikipedia names no cofounder and gives MacKenzie Scott no founding role.
notes: Solo founder, no pair; Wikipedia only.

what_happened: Elon Musk founded SpaceX alone in 2002; Tom Mueller and other early hires are described as employees, not cofounders.
notes: Solo founder, no pair; Wikipedia only.

what_happened: Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded Google in 1998, ran it together, and gave up their Alphabet executive roles (CEO and president) in one joint announcement on 3 December 2019, both staying on the board as controlling shareholders; no split between them is documented.
notes: Fortune notes they kept voting control through special stock and wrote a joint note saying they were 'deeply committed to Google and Alphabet for the long term'.

what_happened: Curtis Priem, Nvidia's chief technical officer since the 1993 founding, retired from the company in 2003 and had sold all his Nvidia shares by 2006; no dispute with Jensen Huang or Chris Malachowsky is documented.
notes: Fortune (5 Apr 2024): Nvidia declined to comment on his departure; Priem told Forbes 'I wish I'd kept a little bit more.' Only friction on record: both Priem and Huang have claimed credit for the company name (Nvidia Wikipedia article). Draft's 'left quietly' confirmed.

what_happened: Bob Miner, who had led Oracle's database development since 1977, gave up that role in December 1992 to run a small advanced-technology group inside Oracle, left the board in October 1993 after a cancer diagnosis, and died in November 1994; he never left the company and no public split with Larry Ellison is documented.
notes: Draft's 'left in 1992 over disagreements' is only partly supported: Wikipedia says Miner 'did not agree with the demands laid upon them by Ellison' about late working hours, and DOAG calls him 'against extremely late hours'; neither describes a resignation, ouster or feud. Business Insider India page (DNS failure) and newspaper obituaries could not be fetched.

what_happened: Ed Oates retired from Oracle in 1996 and bought a home-theater store whose clients later included his former partner Larry Ellison; no conflict is documented.
notes: Miner had died in 1994, so Ellison was the only other cofounder still at Oracle.

what_happened: Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore left Fairchild Semiconductor together and founded Intel in July 1968; they worked together until Noyce died of a heart attack in June 1990, and no split is documented.
notes: Investor Arthur Rock helped incorporate the company but is not listed as a founder in the Intel infobox. ETHW is the IEEE history site (a history profile).

what_happened: Andy Grove joined Intel on the day it was incorporated in 1968 as its third employee and first COO, and later ran the company, but Wikipedia says plainly he 'was not a founder'.
notes: cofounder status disputed in some sources: an ETHW photo caption calls Noyce 'cofounder, along with Andy Grove and Gordon Moore'; Intel's and Grove's Wikipedia articles list only Noyce and Moore.

what_happened: Jack Ma gathered 17 colleagues in his Hangzhou apartment in 1999 to found Alibaba; no split, lawsuit or feud among the 18 cofounders is documented, and Ma's 2020 clash with Chinese regulators (Ant Group IPO blocked, $2.8 billion antitrust fine) was with the state, not with a cofounder.
notes: The Drum page (8 Nov 2018) was fetched with curl because WebFetch returned it empty. Wikipedia names only two other cofounders in passing (Lucy Peng, Trudy Dai). Several of the 18 later moved to other roles; no documented split was found, but a founder-by-founder check was not done. AFP wire via latestly.com (fetched) confirms the apartment founding.

what_happened: Brothers Patrick and John Collison founded Stripe in 2010 and still run it as CEO and president; no split is documented.
notes: Wikipedia infobox says founded 2009, body says 2010.

what_happened: Seven former OpenAI researchers led by Dario and Daniela Amodei founded Anthropic in January 2021 after leaving OpenAI over its direction; Dario Amodei said in May 2024 that all seven cofounders were still at the company, and a 26 October 2026 New York Times profile (republished by The Nightly) still lists all seven in current roles.
notes: cofounder status disputed for Ben Mann: Wikipedia's infobox lists eight cofounders including Mann; the NYT/Nightly piece lists seven without Mann; a May 2024 Yahoo Finance/Benzinga report (https://sg.finance.yahoo.com/news/ai-titans-clash-anthropics-ceo-140012380.html, fetched) quotes Amodei: 'We have seven co-founders... we're all still at the company.' Role changes only: Clark moved to head of public benefit, McCandlish from CTO to chief architect.

notes: The 2009 date comes from Wikipedia; the Gillespie interview (3 Apr 2024) and Lonsdale's own bio (https://blog.joelonsdale.com/about, fetched) do not state a departure year. No major-press article on the departure could be fetched before the search budget ran out. Draft's 'left quietly' confirmed.

notes: Could not verify when or how Gettings left Palantir; no conflict documented anywhere. CB Insights names the RoboteX founder as Adam Gettings, so even that attribution is uncertain.

founder_b: Ma Huateng; Zhang Zhidong (Tony Zhang); Chen Yidan; Xu Chenye
what_happened: Zeng Liqing resigned as Tencent's chief operating officer on 8 June 2007 to 'pursue his personal interests', was named Advisor Emeritus the same day, and became an angel investor backing ex-Tencent founders through Decent Capital; the company called him a core founder who had 'made tremendous contribution', and no dispute is documented.
notes: Zeng has no English Wikipedia article (404), so the company article is given. Tencent's 8 June 2007 press release PDF (https://static.www.tencent.com/storage/uploads/2019/11/09/78befecefd8c5a852eb0fe43e43a5ecb.pdf) was downloaded with curl and read with pdftotext; it is the primary record. Draft's 'left quietly' confirmed.

founder_b: Ma Huateng; Zhang Zhidong (Tony Zhang); Xu Chenye
what_happened: Chen Yidan stepped down as Tencent's chief administrative officer on 20 March 2013 'due to personal reasons and after reaching consensus with the Company's management team', became Advisor Emeritus the next day, stayed honorary chairman of the Tencent Charity Foundation, and founded his own charity foundation.
notes: Not in the draft's list of departures; added. Tencent's HKEX announcement of 20 March 2013 (https://static.www.tencent.com/storage/uploads/2019/11/09/a8a6074c565fc59448685a51a6e9ee55.pdf, curl + pdftotext) is the primary record; Tatler Asia profile (fetched) agrees.

notes: Digitaling (21 Mar 2014, Chinese) reproduces Zhang's letter and Ma's reply. Tencent's HKEX announcement of 19 March 2014 (https://static.www.tencent.com/storage/uploads/2019/11/09/b27cbe17474acee713367342a158b8f5.pdf, curl + pdftotext) is the primary record. Xu Chenye has no English Wikipedia article (404); no departure found for him. Draft's 'left 2014' confirmed.

founder_b: Parker Harris; Dave Moellenhoff; Frank Dominguez
what_happened: Marc Benioff, Parker Harris, Dave Moellenhoff and Frank Dominguez started Salesforce on 8 March 1999 in a rented one-bedroom apartment on San Francisco's Telegraph Hill; Moellenhoff and Dominguez later left without any documented dispute, Harris is still there, and no cofounder split is documented.
notes: Watch item for judgement: in February 2026 Harris criticised Benioff's ICE jokes at the company kickoff ('Marc made a very bad joke'); Wikipedia calls it a public rebuke, while the only fetched report (https://www.el-balad.com/6853890, low-profile outlet) says he spoke at an internal meeting and avoided public criticism. Harris stayed; a one-off rebuke is not a feud under the definition. Only the company's own history page could be fetched for the founding team (vator.tv redirected to an empty substack; SF Chronicle piece failed to load).

founder_b: Bernard Marcus; Arthur Blank; Ron Brill; Ken Langone
what_happened: Pat Farrah, the merchandising cofounder who set up Home Depot's first Atlanta stores, left the company and later came back for a second stint, but the fetched sources disagree on when (Wikipedia: left in the early 1990s 'to pursue his own interests', rejoined 1996; the trade paper HBSDealer, in a search snippet only, says left 1985, rejoined 1995) and none describes the circumstances or any conflict with Marcus or Blank.
notes: Fox Business confirms only that Farrah 'co-founded and invested in Home Depot' (it does not name Ron Brill). HBSDealer's 'The merchant prince' profile (https://www.hbsdealer.com/news/merchant-prince) returned HTTP 403 twice, so its 1985/1995 dates are unconfirmed. The draft's 1985 date and the circumstances could not be verified; no fetched source says he was pushed out.

what_happened: Phil Knight and his Oregon track coach Bill Bowerman each put in $500 to start Blue Ribbon Sports (later Nike) in 1964; Bowerman retired from Nike's board in 1999 and died that December, with Knight calling him 'a hero, leader and most of all teacher'.
notes: Only dispute on record is Blue Ribbon Sports vs. Onitsuka Tiger (1971-72), not between the founders.

what_happened: Zev Siegl left Starbucks in May 1980 after a decade as vice president and director, and the company bought back his 2,541 shares; Baldwin had decided side ventures such as Siegl's Pike Place Teas did not belong in Starbucks, and Siegl, calling himself 'a start-up guy', chose to leave rather than manage a growing company.
notes: A business disagreement over side ventures, not a feud: Siegl later called his partners 'tolerant, interested supporters'. Baldwin and Bowker stayed together until they sold Starbucks in 1987 to keep Peet's. Bowker died 21 Aug 2025 (Telegraph obituary via Yahoo, https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/gordon-bowker-adman-co-founded-050000301.html, fetched).

founder_b: Jerry Baldwin; Gordon Bowker; Zev Siegl
what_happened: Howard Schultz was hired by Starbucks in 1982 as marketing director, left in 1985 to start his Il Giornale cafes, and in 1987 led a group of investors who bought Starbucks from Baldwin and Bowker for $3.8 million; he was never a founder.
notes: Baldwin and Bowker kept Peet's and sold Starbucks; HistoryLink says the board had first voted against hiring Schultz in 1982. Not a cofounder split; the draft is right that Schultz is not a cofounder.

what_happened: Paul Sciarra, Pinterest's CEO on paper, left in April 2012 to become an entrepreneur-in-residence at investor Andreessen Horowitz, saying he would stay on as an adviser and shareholder, and Ben Silbermann, who had already been running the company, became the official CEO.
notes: TechCrunch called the situation 'complicated' (Sciarra had taken a six-week hiatus) but reported no dispute. Draft's 2012 confirmed.

what_happened: Evan Sharp stepped down as Pinterest's chief design and creative officer on 14 October 2021 to join Jony Ive's design firm LoveFrom, writing that he wanted 'to grow as a designer and product builder', and stayed on Pinterest's board as an adviser.
notes: Not in the draft; added for completeness (same pattern as Gebbia). Bloomberg noted the timing coincided with discrimination accusations against Pinterest but did not tie them to Sharp's exit.

what_happened: Joe Gebbia stepped back from his full-time operating role at Airbnb on 21 July 2022 to focus on fatherhood, a complementary product, filmmaking and philanthropy, keeping his board seats at Airbnb and Airbnb.org and becoming an adviser to Chesky and Blecharczyk.
notes: CNBC and Fast Company versions returned 403 to WebFetch. Gebbia joined DOGE in Feb 2025 (Airbnb Wikipedia), prompting boycott calls, but no cofounder dispute is documented. Draft's 2022 confirmed.

what_happened: Jim Clark, fresh from resigning at Silicon Graphics, recruited Marc Andreessen, who had built the Mosaic browser, and the two founded Mosaic Communications (renamed Netscape) on 4 April 1994; no split between them is documented through AOL's 1999 purchase of the company.
notes: IndustryWeek profile is from Dec 1995. Computer History Museum entry (https://www.computerhistory.org/tdih/april/4/, fetched) also names both founders.

what_happened: Brothers Sam and James 'Bud' Walton founded Wal-Mart in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962 and worked together until Sam died in 1992; Bud died in 1995 and no split is documented.
notes: Supermarket News (27 Mar 1995) describes Bud as 'a co-founder, with his late brother Sam'.

what_happened: Jim Sinegal and lawyer Jeff Brotman opened the first Costco warehouse in Seattle in 1983, with Sinegal as long-time CEO and Brotman as chairman until his death on 1 August 2017; no split is documented.
notes: Boston Globe says Brotman 'helped start the Costco chain in 1982'; Wikipedia dates the first warehouse to 15 Sep 1983. Sinegal left the board in 2018.

what_happened: In 1999 Reed Hastings walked into Marc Randolph's office, closed the door and argued with a slide deck that Netflix would be stronger with Hastings as CEO and Randolph as president; Randolph, though stung, agreed, stayed through the 2002 IPO, left in 2003 (Wikipedia says 2002), and calls it 'probably the best decision I ever made at Netflix'.
notes: Borderline case: a founder displaced as CEO by his cofounder, but both describe it as amicable and Randolph credits Hastings; no public statements of acrimony, so not 'broke up' under the definition. Departure year conflicts: Wikipedia 2002, Entrepreneur and the draft 2003. Hastings's line per Randolph: 'I'm proposing that we run the company together.'

what_happened: Dmitri Alperovitch stepped down as CrowdStrike's CTO in February 2020 to start the nonprofit Silverado Policy Accelerator; CEO George Kurtz thanked him for eight years of 'commitment' and said 'We wish him well', and Michael Sentonas took over as CTO.
notes: Third cofounder Gregg Marston (CFO) retired; Wikipedia lists him as a cofounder and the draft omits him. Draft's 2020 confirmed.

what_happened: Andy Bechtolsheim, Stanford professor David Cheriton and Ken Duda founded Arastra (renamed Arista Networks) in 2004; Bechtolsheim and Duda are still listed as founders on Arista's management page, Cheriton was its chief scientist, and no split is documented.
notes: Cheriton no longer appears on Arista's management page; aggregator profiles put his formal role (Director & Chief Scientific Officer) at 2012-2014 and his Wikipedia article (fetched) gives no departure date or reason; could not verify with a news source (O'Reilly 'Arista Warrior' chapter returned 403). Arista's Wikipedia article carries an LLM-text warning. Only a company page could be fetched for the founding team.

what_happened: After a board special committee's review of backdated stock options, Marvell announced on 7 May 2007 that cofounder Weili Dai would no longer serve as executive vice president, chief operating officer, or director, keeping only a non-management marketing job, while her husband Sehat Sutardja stayed on as CEO and gave up the chairman title.
notes: Partial ouster: she stayed at the company in a non-management role. Founder-versus-board event; Dai and Sutardja are married, so no split between the cofounders.

what_happened: On 5 April 2016, after an audit-committee probe that found no fraud but 'significant pressure' from management on sales teams to meet revenue targets, and two months after activist Starboard Value took a stake, Marvell announced that CEO Sehat Sutardja and president Weili Dai were stepping down; Dai's Wikipedia article calls it an ouster.
notes: Married couple removed together, so not a split between them. Reuters said both initially kept board seats, Sutardja as chairman; Starboard later placed three directors and Matt Murphy became CEO in July 2016. Pantas Sutardja (Sehat's brother) is the third cofounder; his status at the time was not checked. Marvell company article also fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marvell_Technology

what_happened: Lorber cofounded Analog Devices with his MIT roommate Ray Stata in 1965, and when the company went public in 1969 he sold half his stock and moved on to other ventures, later founding Copley Controls.
notes: No dispute documented. MIT News (https://news.mit.edu/1997/company-0305) also names Richard Burwen as a third founder; Wikipedia lists only Stata and Lorber. Company article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analog_Devices

what_happened: Mehrotra, SanDisk's CEO from 2011 after cofounder Eli Harari retired, ran the company until Western Digital bought it in May 2016, joined WD's board, and left that board in February 2017 saying the time was right to evaluate his next challenge; he became Micron's CEO three months later.
notes: No dispute documented among the three founders. Harari's retirement (Mehrotra took over as CEO in 2011) and Yuan's later role were not separately verified. Founding team profile: https://ethw.org/Jack_Yuan; company article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SanDisk; Harari article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eli_Harari

what_happened: Mera and her then-husband Amancio Ortega opened the first Zara store in A Coruña in 1975; they divorced in 1986, and she kept about 7% of Inditex (6.99% at her death in 2013), with no business dispute between them reported.
notes: Divorce, not a business feud: no lawsuit or public dispute found in any fetched source. News reports disagree on her stake (CBS 5.1%, AP and Madrid filings 6.99%). A search snippet said she left the Inditex board in 2004 (not verified by a fetched source). Company article: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inditex
